quests.explanation: Borrowed directly from French, this word keeps an unusual spelling pattern, especially the 'eur' ending pronounced 'er.'
Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-able' is a standard pattern, as in 'negotiate' to 'negotiable.'
When an adjective ends in '-le,' the noun form sometimes changes to '-ility,' as in 'liable' to 'liability.'

quests.hint: Tricky spelling: BU-REAU-CRA-CY, with a silent letter pattern in 'reau.'
quests.explanation: Borrowed from French 'bureau' (office) plus Greek 'kratos' (power), this word describes rule through administrative offices.
This business term describes someone who 'holds a stake' (interest) in the outcome of a decision or company.
Related to 'subsidy' (financial support), a subsidiary is a company controlled by, and often supported by, a larger parent company.
When a verb ends in '-ire,' the noun form sometimes changes to '-isition,' as in 'acquire' to 'acquisition.'
This business term describes finding a 'source' for work 'outside' your own company, combining two familiar words.
Borrowed from French 'revenir' (to return), revenue is literally the money that 'returns' to a business from sales.
The suffix '-iture' (related to '-ure') turns the verb 'expend' (to spend) into a noun describing total spending.
The root 'chron' relates to time (as in 'chronological'), so a chronic condition is one that persists over a long 'time.'
The suffix '-ic' turns the noun 'allergy' into an adjective describing someone who has that reaction.
From Greek 'metabole' (change), metabolism describes the chemical 'changes' your body constantly performs to convert food into energy.
The prefix 'in-' means 'not,' and 'somnia' relates to Latin 'somnus' (sleep) — insomnia is literally 'not sleeping.'
The suffix '-ist' describes a person devoted to a field, as in 'nutrition' becoming the profession 'nutritionist.'
The suffix '-ize' turns the noun 'priority' into a verb meaning to treat something as more important.
This vivid compound word describes 'shooting' (aiming directly at) the source of 'trouble' in a system.
Just as a physical firewall stops flames from spreading between rooms, a digital firewall blocks harmful data from spreading between networks.
Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-ation' follows the familiar pattern from 'navigate' and 'graduate.'
The suffix '-ivity' turns the verb 'connect' into an abstract noun describing the ability or quality of being connected.
Similar to 'layover,' a stopover describes a brief stop made 'over' the course of a longer journey.
The prefix 'dis-' reverses 'embark' (to board), so to disembark means to get off a ship, plane, or train.

quests.hint: It's related to 'hospital' — remember the 'i': HOS-PI-TAL-I-TY.
quests.explanation: Sharing a root with 'hospital,' both words come from Latin 'hospes' (host or guest), focused on welcoming people warmly.
This is the verb form of 'accommodation,' and it's commonly misspelled by missing one of the two double letters.
Borrowed directly from French, 'concierge' keeps its original pronunciation and spelling pattern for this hotel-service role.

quests.hint: It's related to 'itinerary' — describes someone always traveling: I-TIN-ER-ANT.
quests.explanation: Sharing a root with 'itinerary,' 'itinerant' describes a person, like a traveling worker, who moves from place to place.

quests.hint: Remember the French spelling: PRE-MIERE, not 'premier' (which is a different word).
quests.explanation: 'Premiere' (the first showing of a film) and 'premier' (a top leader, or 'first' in rank) are easily confused — note the extra 'e' at the end.
Adding '-er' to the noun 'choreography' creates the title for the person who creates the dance moves.
The root 'tography' relates to Greek 'graphein' (to write or record), so cinematography is literally 'writing' with a film camera.
This compound word describes a 'stage' (large indoor set) specially built and soundproofed for filming with controlled audio.
